props.title: Smoke
props.initialSlug: Lives intersect at a Brooklyn tobacco shop

sections.content: **Smoke** (1995) represents indie filmmaking at its most thoughtfully crafted. Director Wayne Wang and writer Paul Auster weave an intricate tapestry of Brooklyn life centered around Auggie Wren's tobacco shop. The film's power lies in its interconnected stories and Harvey Keitel's nuanced performance as Auggie, who photographs his shop's corner every morning at the same time - a meditation on observation and routine that influenced later slice-of-life indies like **Coffee and Cigarettes** (2003) and **Paterson** (2016).

sections.content: The mid-90s marked a golden age for American independent cinema focused on urban life and everyday philosophy. **Smoke** shares DNA with Richard Linklater's **Before Sunrise** (1995) in its love of conversation and chance encounters. Both films trust in the power of dialogue and human connection, letting characters breathe and stories unfold naturally. Wang's direction shows clear influence from earlier character studies like John Cassavetes' **Shadows** (1959), particularly in its authentic portrayal of city life.

The film's structure - with its interlocking stories and emphasis on storytelling itself - created a template for later ensemble pieces. You can trace its influence through works like **Things You Can Tell Just by Looking at Her** (2000) and **13 Conversations About One Thing** (2001). The way **Smoke** uses its Brooklyn location as both setting and character would later be echoed in films like **Little Men** (2016) and **Brooklyn** (2015). sections.content: At its heart, **Smoke** is about the power of stories - both those we tell others and those we tell ourselves. This meta-narrative approach influenced later works like **The Sweet Hereafter** (1997) and **Big Fish** (2003). The famous Christmas story sequence that closes the film demonstrates how cinema can capture the oral tradition, something later explored in films like **Volver** (2006) and **Stories We Tell** (2012).
